claim: ArfA rescues ribosomes stalled on truncated mRNAs by recruiting release factor RF2.
source: ArfA rescues ribosomes stalled on truncated mRNAs by recruiting release factor RF2, which normally binds stop codons to catalyze peptide release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of ArfA, supported by the authors' structural work and previous literature.

claim: RF2 normally binds stop codons to catalyze peptide release.
source: ArfA rescues ribosomes stalled on truncated mRNAs by recruiting release factor RF2, which normally binds stop codons to catalyze peptide release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RF2 function in canonical translation termination.

claim: Two 3.2 Å resolution cryo-EM structures of the 70S ribosome with ArfA•RF2 in the A site were determined from a single sample.
source: We report two 3.2 Å resolution cryo-EM structures – determined from a single sample – of the 70S ribosome with ArfA•RF2 in the A site.
evidence: The resolution and number of structures are directly stated and supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in methods.

claim: In both states, the ArfA C-terminus occupies the mRNA tunnel downstream of the A site.
source: In both states, the ArfA C-terminus occupies the mRNA tunnel downstream of the A site.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: One state contains a compact inactive RF2 conformation.
source: One state contains a compact inactive RF2 conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by Structure I in the cryo-EM data.

claim: Ordering of the ArfA N-terminus in the second state rearranges RF2 into an extended conformation that docks the catalytic GGQ motif into the peptidyl-transferase center.
source: Ordering of the ArfA N-terminus in the second state rearranges RF2 into an extended conformation that docks the catalytic GGQ motif into the peptidyl-transferase center.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by Structure II in the cryo-EM data.

claim: ArfA 'senses' the vacant mRNA tunnel and activates RF2 to mediate peptide release without a stop codon.
source: The structures demonstrate how ArfA 'senses' the vacant mRNA tunnel and activates RF2 to mediate peptide release without a stop codon, allowing stalled ribosomes to be recycled.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A translating ribosome stalls when it encounters the end of a non-stop mRNA.
source: A translating ribosome stalls when it encounters the end of a non-stop mRNA, truncated during cellular stress or homeostasis, by premature transcription termination or mRNA cleavage or other mechanisms (Hayes and Keiler, 2010; Keiler, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The stalled ribosome contains peptidyl-tRNA in the P site, whereas the aminoacyl-tRNA (A) site is unoccupied.
source: The stalled ribosome contains peptidyl-tRNA in the P site, whereas the aminoacyl-tRNA (A) site is unoccupied (Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Bacteria have evolved ribosome-rescue pathways to release the nascent peptide and re-enable the stalled ribosome for translation.
source: Bacteria have evolved ribosome-rescue pathways to release the nascent peptide and re-enable the stalled ribosome for translation (for a review, see ref. [Keiler, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The ArfA pathway is essential in trans-translation-deficient cells.
source: The ArfA (alternative rescue factor A) pathway is essential in trans-translation-deficient cells (Chadani et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ArfA is thought to function as a backup mechanism for trans-translation in enterobacteria.
source: and is thought to function as a backup mechanism for trans-translation in enterobacteria (Garza-Sánchez et al., 2011; Chadani et al., 2011; Schaub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: ArfA is a small protein (~70 aa in most organisms).
source: ArfA is a small protein (~70 aa in most organisms), with only 47 amino acids sufficient for function, as shown for E. coli ArfA truncations (Garza-Sánchez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Only 47 amino acids are sufficient for ArfA function, as shown for E. coli ArfA truncations.
source: ArfA is a small protein (~70 aa in most organisms), with only 47 amino acids sufficient for function, as shown for E. coli ArfA truncations (Garza-Sánchez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ArfA recruits release factor RF2 to rescue stalled ribosomes.
source: ArfA recruits release factor RF2 to rescue stalled ribosomes (Chadani et al., 2012; Shimizu, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RF2 normally mediates translation termination at UGA or UAA stop codons.
source: RF2 normally mediates translation termination at UGA or UAA stop codons by binding the stop codon and catalyzing peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis and release of the nascent peptide (Craigen and Caskey, 1987; Korostelev, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RF2 has remarkable specificity toward stop codons.
source: RF2 has remarkable specificity toward stop codons (Freistroffer et al., 2000)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RF2 does not function alone on truncated mRNA.
source: and does not function alone on truncated mRNA (Chadani et al., 2012; Shimizu, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Unsupervised classification of a single cryo-EM dataset using FREALIGN revealed two ribosome structures with both ArfA and RF2 bound in the A site.
source: Unsupervised classification of a single cryo-EM dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) using FREALIGN (Grigorieff, 2016) revealed two ribosome structures with both ArfA and RF2 bound in the A site (Structures I and II; Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the cryo-EM data processing results shown in figures and table.

claim: Structure I contains a compact RF2 and is represented by ~26% of ribosome particles in the cryo-EM dataset.
source: Structure I contains a compact RF2 (Figure 1A and C) and is represented by ~26% of ribosome particles in the cryo-EM dataset.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the classification results and structural data.

claim: Structure II contains an extended RF2 and represents ~18% of ribosomes.
source: Structure II contains an extended RF2 (Figure 1B and D; ~18% of ribosomes).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the classification results and structural data.

claim: Both structures contain tRNAs in the P and E (exit) sites and adopt a non-rotated conformation.
source: Both structures contain tRNAs in the P and E (exit) sites and adopt a non-rotated conformation (Yusupov et al., 2001; Korostelev et al., 2006; Selmer et al., 2006), similar to that in translation termination complexes (Korostelev et al., 2008; Laurberg et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and comparison with cited structures.

claim: High-resolution maps allowed de novo modeling of ArfA.
source: High-resolution maps (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5) allowed de novo modeling of ArfA (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated and supported by the cryo-EM density maps shown in figures.

claim: High-resolution maps allowed detailed structure determination of RF2 in each ribosome structure.
source: High-resolution maps (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5) allowed de novo modeling of ArfA (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and detailed structure determination of RF2 (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4) in each ribosome structure.
evidence: This is stated and supported by the cryo-EM density maps shown in figures.

claim: Sequence alignment of several hundreds of bacterial ArfA homologs reveals conserved hydrophobic N-terminal and positively charged C-terminal regions.
source: Sequence alignment of several hundreds of bacterial ArfA homologs reveals conserved hydrophobic N-terminal and positively charged C-terminal regions (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated and supported by the sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The high conservation of N-terminal and C-terminal regions implicates their functions in protein and RNA interactions, respectively.
source: The high conservation of these regions implicates their functions in protein and RNA interactions, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequence conservation patterns observed.

claim: In Structures I and II, the conformations of the N-terminal region differ.
source: In Structures I and II, the conformations of the N-terminal region differ as described in the following sections, but the rest of ArfA is similar.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison of the two states.

claim: The mid-region of ArfA (His21 to Glu30) lies in the A site.
source: The mid-region of ArfA (His21 to Glu30; E. coli numbering is used) lies in the A site (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated and supported by the structural data shown in figures.

claim: ArfA leaves a ~12 Å gap in the codon-binding region, sufficient to accommodate one or two nucleotides of mRNA following the P-site codon but not a longer mRNA.
source: ArfA leaves a ~12 Å gap in the codon-binding region, sufficient to accommodate one or two nucleotides of mRNA following the P-site codon but not a longer mRNA, consistent with the reduced efficiency of ArfA-mediated release on mRNAs that extend three or more nucleotides beyond the P site (Shimizu, 2012; Zeng and Jin, 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on structural measurements and is consistent with cited biochemical data.

claim: The C-terminal region of ArfA occupies the mRNA tunnel between the head and body of the 30S subunit.
source: The C-terminal region of ArfA occupies the mRNA tunnel between the head and body of the 30S subunit (Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 2), as suggested by previous hydroxyl-radical probing studies (Kurita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on structural data and is consistent with cited biochemical studies.

claim: ArfA is stabilized by electrostatic interactions, as positively charged amino acids comprise nearly half of the ArfA residues within the mRNA tunnel (aa 31–48).
source: ArfA is stabilized by electrostatic interactions, as positively charged amino acids comprise nearly half of the ArfA residues within the mRNA tunnel (aa 31–48; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and sequence analysis.

claim: ArfA residues Lys44 to Arg48 approach the mRNA tunnel entry at the solvent side of the 30S subunit, formed by 16S rRNA and proteins S3, S4 and S5.
source: ArfA residues Lys44 to Arg48 approach the mRNA tunnel entry at the solvent side of the 30S subunit, formed by 16S rRNA and proteins S3, S4 and S5 (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The tail of ArfA appears to form a short α-helix (aa ~50–55) next to S5.
source: Consistent with ArfA structure prediction (Kim et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2015), the tail of ArfA appears to form a short α-helix (aa ~50–55) next to S5; however, the resolution of the map is not sufficient to build an unambiguous structural model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and structure prediction, with acknowledgment of limited resolution.

claim: The resolution of the map is not sufficient to build an unambiguous structural model for the C-terminal α-helix of ArfA.
source: Consistent with ArfA structure prediction (Kim et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2015), the tail of ArfA appears to form a short α-helix (aa ~50–55) next to S5; however, the resolution of the map is not sufficient to build an unambiguous structural model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated regarding the limitations of the structural data.

claim: Conformational disorder of the C-terminus at the entrance to the mRNA tunnel is suggested.
source: This suggests conformational disorder of the C-terminus at the entrance to the mRNA tunnel.
evidence: This is inferred from the limited resolution of the density for this region.

claim: The structures are consistent with biochemical studies showing that ArfA is functional with a C-terminal truncation at Asn47, but further shortening inactivates ArfA.
source: Our structures are consistent with biochemical studies (Chadani et al., 2011), which showed that ArfA is functional with a C-terminal truncation at Asn47, but further shortening inactivates ArfA.
evidence: This is stated as consistency between the structural data and cited biochemical studies.

claim: Truncations following Met40 abrogate ArfA-mediated release by reducing ArfA affinity for the 70S ribosome.
source: In particular, truncations following Met40—removing at least five basic amino acids that bind in the tunnel—abrogate ArfA-mediated release by reducing ArfA affinity for the 70S ribosome (Chadani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited biochemical studies and is explained by the structural observations.

claim: ArfB and SmpB mediate alternative rescue pathways.
source: We compared ArfA with proteins ArfB (also known as YaeJ; [Gagnon et al., 2012]) and SmpB (Neubauer et al., 2012; Ramrath et al., 2012), which mediate alternative rescue pathways (reviewed in [Keiler, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In ArfB-mediated release and SmpB-mediated trans-translation, the proteins sense the stalled ribosomes by occupying the mRNA tunnel.
source: In ArfB-mediated release and SmpB-mediated trans-translation, the proteins sense the stalled ribosomes by occupying the mRNA tunnel (Gagnon et al., 2012; Neubauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Each of ArfA, ArfB, and SmpB interacts with the mRNA tunnel differently.
source: Consistent with sequence divergence among the C-termini of ArfA, ArfB, and SmpB, however, each interacts with the mRNA tunnel differently.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison and sequence analysis.

claim: ArfB performs peptide release when its C-terminus forms a long α-helix in the tunnel.
source: ArfB performs peptide release when its C-terminus forms a long α-helix in the tunnel (Gagnon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SmpB bound with tmRNA forms a shorter α-helix, well-resolved near the mRNA entry at the 30S solvent surface.
source: SmpB bound with tmRNA in preparation for trans-translation, forms a shorter α-helix, well-resolved near the mRNA entry at the 30S solvent surface (Neubauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SmpB is similar to ArfA in that both proteins are sensitive to the mRNA occupancy of the A site.
source: SmpB is similar to ArfA in that both proteins are sensitive to the mRNA occupancy of the A site (Ivanova et al., 2004; Shimizu, 2012; Zeng and Jin, 2016)
evidence: This is stated based on comparison and supported by citations.

claim: ArfB can function on stalled ribosomes with either the vacant or occupied A site.
source: whereas ArfB can function on stalled ribosomes with either the vacant or occupied A site (Handa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Diverged sequences, structures and binding modes of ArfA, ArfB, and SmpB likely reflect distinct affinities and sensitivities to stress conditions.
source: Diverged sequences, structures and binding modes of these proteins likely reflect distinct affinities and sensitivities to stress conditions, in keeping with their roles in mediating distinct ribosome rescue pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural and functional comparisons.

claim: In Structure I, only the central and C-terminal parts of ArfA are visible, indicating that the N-terminal region (aa 2–16) is disordered.
source: In Structure I, only the central and C-terminal parts of ArfA are visible, indicating that the N-terminal region (aa 2–16) is disordered.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM density observations.

claim: RF2 adopts a compact conformation in Structure I similar to that of free (ribosome-unbound) RF2 observed in crystal structures.
source: RF2 adopts a compact conformation (Figure 3A) similar to that of free (ribosome-unbound) RF2 observed in crystal structures (Figure 3B) (Vestergaard et al., 2001; Zoldák et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison with cited crystal structures.

claim: In canonical termination complexes formed on stop codons, release factors have only been observed in an extended (open) conformation.
source: By contrast, in canonical termination complexes formed on stop codons, release factors have only been observed in an extended (open) conformation (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During translation termination, codon-recognition determinants in domain 2 (including the conserved 205SPF207 motif) of RF2 bind the stop codon in the A site of the 30S subunit.
source: During translation termination, codon-recognition determinants in domain 2 (including the conserved 205SPF207 motif) of RF2 bind the stop codon in the A site of the 30S subunit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about canonical termination.

claim: Helix α7 of domain 3 bridges the ribosomal subunits, placing the catalytic GGQ motif of domain 3 within the peptidyl-transferase center of the 50S subunit during translation termination.
source: Helix α7 of domain 3 bridges the ribosomal subunits, placing the catalytic GGQ motif of domain 3 within the peptidyl-transferase center of the 50S subunit (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the ArfA-bound Structure I, helix α7 packs on the β-sheet of domain 2 near the 30S subunit.
source: In the ArfA-bound Structure I, however, helix α7 packs on the β-sheet of domain 2 near the 30S subunit (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: In the compact conformation of Structure I, the loop that contains the 250GGQ252 motif of RF2 lies to the side of the β-sheet of domain 2, facing the anticodon-stem loop and the D stem of the P-site tRNA.
source: In this compact conformation, the loop that contains the 250GGQ252 motif of RF2 lies to the side of the β-sheet (near aa 165–168) of domain 2, facing the anticodon-stem loop and the D stem of the P-site tRNA.
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations.

claim: The GGQ motif is roughly 70 Å away from its catalytically engaged position within the peptidyl-transferase center in Structure I.
source: As such, the GGQ motif is roughly 70 Å away from its catalytically engaged position within the peptidyl-transferase center (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated based on structural measurements shown in figures.

claim: Poor resolution of the catalytic GGQ residues at the tip of the loop suggests local structural flexibility.
source: Poor resolution of the catalytic GGQ residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) at the tip of the loop suggests local structural flexibility, similar to that seen in crystal structures of free release factors (Vestergaard et al., 2001; Shin et al., 2004; Zoldák et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM density quality and comparison with cited crystal structures.

claim: The codon-recognition domain 2 of RF2 is positioned differently from that in canonical termination complexes in Structure I.
source: The codon-recognition domain 2 of RF2 is positioned differently from that in canonical termination complexes.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison.

claim: The domain 2 is withdrawn from the A site, such that the SPF motif and other codon-recognition residues lie ~5 Å away from their positions in termination complexes bound to a stop codon.
source: The domain is withdrawn from the A site, such that the SPF motif and other codon-recognition residues lie ~5 Å away from their positions in termination complexes bound to a stop codon (Figure 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated based on structural measurements and comparison.

claim: The mid-region of ArfA is sandwiched between domain 2 of RF2 and the decoding center.
source: This position results from the mid-region of ArfA being sandwiched between domain 2 of RF2 and the decoding center.
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations.

claim: The backbone of ArfA residues 25–29 binds to RF2 residues 213–217 within the β-sheet of domain 2, forming an extended β-sheet platform.
source: Here, the backbone of ArfA residues 25–29 binds to RF2 residues 213–217 within the β-sheet of domain 2 (Figure 1E), forming an extended β-sheet platform (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The conformation of the decoding center in Structure I differs from that in canonical termination complexes.
source: The conformation of the decoding center in Structure I differs from that in canonical termination complexes.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison.

claim: In 70S termination complexes, the decoding center interacts with the switch loop of RF2 (aa 315–323), which bridges the codon-recognition and catalytic domains.
source: In 70S termination complexes, the decoding center interacts with the switch loop of RF2 (aa 315–323), which bridges the codon-recognition and catalytic domains (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A1492 bulges from helix 44 (h44) of 16S rRNA and stacks on conserved Trp319 of the switch loop in canonical termination complexes.
source: A1492 bulges from helix 44 (h44) of 16S rRNA and stacks on conserved Trp319 of the switch loop (Figure 4C), stabilizing the extended conformation of RF2 on the ribosome (Figure 4F) (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: In Structure I, A1492 and A1493 lie inside h44 and are sandwiched between Pro23 of ArfA and A1913 of helix 69 of 23S rRNA.
source: In Structure I, however, A1492 and A1493 lie inside h44 and are sandwiched between Pro23 of ArfA and A1913 of helix 69 of 23S rRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The RF2 switch loop is poorly ordered in Structure I.
source: The RF2 switch loop is poorly ordered.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM density quality.

claim: Putative density suggests that Trp319 is placed >10 Å away from its position in the termination complex and does not contact the decoding-center nucleotides in Structure I.
source: Putative density suggests that Trp319 is placed >10 Å away from its position in the termination complex and does not contact the decoding-center nucleotides (Figure 4D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and measurements shown in figures.

claim: Structure I describes a 70S rescue complex in which ArfA stabilizes a compact form of RF2 resembling that of free RF2.
source: Taken together, Structure I describes a 70S rescue complex in which ArfA stabilizes a compact form of RF2 resembling that of free RF2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the structural observations.

claim: The remote position of RF2's catalytic GGQ motif away from the peptidyl-transferase center indicates that Structure I represents an inactive form of the 70S rescue complex.
source: The remote position of RF2's catalytic GGQ motif—away from the peptidyl-transferase center—indicates that Structure I represents an inactive form of the 70S rescue complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural observations.

claim: Structure II features an extended conformation of RF2.
source: Structure II features an extended conformation of RF2 (Figures 1B, 3C and D), stabilized by interactions with the ordered N-terminal region of ArfA (Figures 2, 4B and E).
evidence: This is stated and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The extended conformation of RF2 in Structure II is stabilized by interactions with the ordered N-terminal region of ArfA.
source: Structure II features an extended conformation of RF2 (Figures 1B, 3C and D), stabilized by interactions with the ordered N-terminal region of ArfA (Figures 2, 4B and E).
evidence: This is stated and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The N-terminus of ArfA forms a minidomain, which packs between helix 69 of 23S rRNA, the β-sheet of domain 2, and extended helix α7 of RF2.
source: The N-terminus of ArfA forms a minidomain, which packs between helix 69 of 23S rRNA, the β-sheet of domain 2, and extended helix α7 of RF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The tip of the ArfA minidomain (at aa 12–13) protrudes from the decoding center toward the 50S subunit.
source: The tip of the ArfA minidomain (at aa 12–13) protrudes from the decoding center toward the 50S subunit, whereas the N-terminus folds back toward the decoding center, consistent with recent hydroxyl-radical probing studies (Kurita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and is consistent with cited biochemical studies.

claim: Thr7 and Lys8 of ArfA bind h44 (at A1410) of 16S rRNA.
source: Here, Thr7 and Lys8 bind h44 (at A1410) of 16S rRNA and the N-terminal amino acids bind the β-sheet of S12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The N-terminal amino acids of ArfA bind the β-sheet of S12.
source: Here, Thr7 and Lys8 bind h44 (at A1410) of 16S rRNA and the N-terminal amino acids bind the β-sheet of S12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: A hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain of ArfA is formed by Leu19, Leu24, and Phe25.
source: A hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain of ArfA (Figure 2B) — formed by Leu19, Leu24, and Phe25—binds RF2 at Trp319 of the rearranged switch loop (Figure 4B and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain of ArfA binds RF2 at Trp319 of the rearranged switch loop.
source: A hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain of ArfA (Figure 2B) — formed by Leu19, Leu24, and Phe25—binds RF2 at Trp319 of the rearranged switch loop (Figure 4B and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: These interactions explain the strict dependence of ArfA on RF2, rather than on the second release factor RF1.
source: These interactions explain the strict dependence of ArfA on RF2, rather than on the second release factor RF1 (Chadani et al., 2012; Shimizu, 2012), whose switch loop is diverged from that of RF2 and lacks tryptophan (Korostelev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural observations and is consistent with cited biochemical studies.

claim: The switch loop of RF1 is diverged from that of RF2 and lacks tryptophan.
source: These interactions explain the strict dependence of ArfA on RF2, rather than on the second release factor RF1 (Chadani et al., 2012; Shimizu, 2012), whose switch loop is diverged from that of RF2 and lacks tryptophan (Korostelev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain also binds RF2 at Val198 and Phe217 of the β-sheet of the codon-recognition domain 2.
source: The hydrophobic patch in the N-terminal minidomain also binds RF2 at Val198 and Phe217 of the β-sheet of the codon-recognition domain 2 (Figure 4B and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: In Structure II, the codon-recognition domain of RF2 partially settles into the decoding center, but remains ~3 Å from its position in canonical termination complexes bound to a stop codon.
source: In this configuration, the codon-recognition domain of RF2 partially settles into the decoding center, but remains ~3 Å from its position in canonical termination complexes bound to a stop codon.
evidence: This is stated based on structural measurements and comparison.

claim: The SPF motif remains unbound to the ribosome or ArfA in Structure II.
source: As in Structure I, the SPF motif remains unbound to the ribosome or ArfA.
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations.

claim: Mutation of SPF motif residues do not disrupt ArfA-mediated peptide release.
source: This observation explains why mutation of SPF motif residues—critical for stop-codon recognition—do not disrupt ArfA-mediated peptide release (Chadani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural observations and is consistent with cited biochemical studies.

claim: The position of the ArfA N-terminal minidomain between RF2's domain 2 and helix α7 of domain 3 results in docking of domain 3 into the peptidyl-transferase center.
source: The position of the ArfA N-terminal minidomain between RF2's domain 2 and helix α7 of domain 3 results in docking of domain 3 into the peptidyl-transferase center (Figures 1, 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures.

claim: The opening of domain 3 is accompanied by movement of domain 1 of RF2.
source: The opening of domain 3 is accompanied by movement of domain 1 of RF2 (Figure 3E), which binds the L11 stalk and shifts the L11 stalk by ~7 Å toward the A site, relative to that in Structure I (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and measurements shown in figures.

claim: Domain 1 of RF2 binds the L11 stalk and shifts the L11 stalk by ~7 Å toward the A site, relative to that in Structure I.
source: The opening of domain 3 is accompanied by movement of domain 1 of RF2 (Figure 3E), which binds the L11 stalk and shifts the L11 stalk by ~7 Å toward the A site, relative to that in Structure I (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations and measurements shown in figures.

claim: The coordinated shift of L11 and domain 1 likely contribute to the movement of domain 3 toward the PTC.
source: The coordinated shift of L11 and domain 1 likely contribute to the movement of domain 3 toward the PTC, echoing the involvement of the L11 stalk in canonical termination by RF2 (Xu et al., 2002; Sato et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural observations and is consistent with cited studies on canonical termination.

claim: The catalytic GGQ motif of domain 3 binds in the peptidyl-transferase center with the catalytic backbone amide of Gln252 proximal to the ribose of the terminal A76 of P-site tRNA.
source: The catalytic GGQ motif of domain 3 binds in the peptidyl-transferase center with the catalytic backbone amide of Gln252 (Korostelev et al., 2008; Santos et al., 2013) proximal to the ribose of the terminal A76 of P-site tRNA (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on structural observations shown in figures and is consistent with cited studies on the catalytic mechanism.

claim: The conformation of the peptidyl-transferase center is nearly identical to that seen in canonical translation termination complexes.
source: The conformation of the peptidyl-transferase center is nearly identical to that seen in canonical translation termination complexes (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison with cited structures.

claim: Structure II represents an activated state of the ArfA•RF2-bound ribosome rescue complex.
source: Structure II therefore represents an activated state of the ArfA•RF2-bound ribosome rescue complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural observations.

claim: Structures I and II are in agreement with previous biochemical and mutagenesis studies.
